headline: Bass crash the Stratford Shoal rip as Sound water hits perfect 68 degrees
subhead: New moon spring tides are flushing bait through the narrows and stacking stripers on the edges.
body_markdown:
The Central Sound is firing right now, and it all comes down to that magic number: 68 degrees. The buoys are telling the story I've been waiting for all month — water temps have settled into that sweet spot where everything clicks. From the Norwalk Islands to Port Jeff, the thermometer is reading 68 to 68.2, and the fish are responding like clockwork.

I've been watching the Stratford Shoal rip closely this week, and it's become a striper magnet. The new moon on Friday is pushing serious water through the narrows, creating those current seams that concentrate bait and trigger feeding. White bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range are absolutely crushing it on the edges of the rip. Cast up-current, let it sink to the bottom, then work it back with slow lifts and drops. The bass are sitting in 25 to 35 feet, facing into the flow and ambushing anything that drifts down.

The key is positioning yourself correctly relative to the current. These spring tides are moving water fast — sometimes too fast for lighter jigs to maintain bottom contact. When the current's screaming, bump up to that 2-ounce bucktail and add a strip of silver Mylar for extra flash. The fish are eating on the fall, so keep that bottom contact and feel for the tick.

Across the Sound, the Middle Ground Light area has been producing steady action on fluke. The 4-foot drop from the shallow bar into 25 feet is holding fish, and they're responding to pink and white Gulp trailers on 3/4-ounce bucktails. The triangle method is working perfectly here — I'm rotating between three connected spots when one goes quiet. First drift tells you everything you need to know about whether fish are present.

What's really got me excited is the bait situation. Spearing are thick along the Connecticut shoreline, and I'm seeing good marks of bunker moving through the shipping channels. The larger bunker are pushing into deeper water as the Sound warms, which explains why the bass fishing has been so consistent in that 25 to 35-foot zone around structure.

The Norwalk Islands circuit is producing mixed bags of bass and blues on the rocky edges. Seven-inch white pencil poppers are working the early morning bite when the water's calm, but once the sun gets up, switch to bucktails and work the current breaks around the islands. The fish are holding tight to structure, so get your lures close to the rocks.

Port Jefferson Harbor has been a sleeper spot this week. The ferry terminal area in deeper water is holding fish, and the slightly green tint to the water tells me the bait is moving and the fish are paying attention. Live peanut bunker on fishfinder rigs are producing when worked tight to the pilings on the outgoing tide.

Looking at the conditions, this new moon period is setting up perfectly. These spring tides are going to flush massive amounts of bait out of the harbors and bays, creating feeding opportunities throughout the Sound. The strong currents can be challenging, but that's when the fish really get aggressive on the baitfish that lose control in the flow.

The weather pattern looks stable through the weekend with light winds, which means you can work the rips effectively without getting beat up. Water temps should hold steady in that productive 68-degree range, keeping the fish active and feeding.

For the week ahead, I'm watching for the tide changes around the full moon. These big water movements are going to concentrate bait and create those feeding windows where everything happens at once. Focus on the current edges, keep your bucktails in contact with the bottom, and be ready to move when the action shifts. The Central Sound is in prime time right now.
